objectives: Explain how zero waste looks at waste.
Explain the numbers about city waste.
Explain why plastic waste is worrying.
Use expect … to and the passive.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter defines waste in two ways and gives the key numbers. A number line (2023 → 2050) and a short list of materials help learners hold the facts before the detailed chapters.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The zero waste idea does not see waste as just leftovers; it sees it as the result of poor planning.
62 percent is the waste that is treated, not the waste that is recycled.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: expect + object + to · present simple passive (is treated) · make up / end up
Notice (Activity 1): Experts expect this number to reach 3.8 billion tons by 2050.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *expect this number reaching · *waste are treated.
Use (Activity 4): what is in our bin?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Numbers: two point three billion tons; three point eight billion.
Stress: fa-CIL-i-ties, or-GAN-ic, con-SUME, WOR-ry-ing.
beforeReading: Ask: “Is waste only what is left over, or something more?”
duringReading: First reading: How does zero waste look at waste?
Second reading: complete the number line.
Find why plastic waste is worrying.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Number line; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: what is in our bin?; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is the difference between the two ideas of waste?
What makes up the largest part of city waste?
Why is the rise in plastic waste worrying?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Different Way” and “62 Percent” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: consume, solid waste, expect, facility, organic, worrying, end up.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the number line with the years written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that compares the two ideas of waste.

formativeAssessment: Uses expect … to or the passive correctly.
expectedResponses: The zero waste idea sees waste as the result of poor product planning. In 2023, the world produced 2.3 billion tons of city waste, and experts expect this number to reach 3.8 billion tons by 2050.
content.transferTask: Write about the waste in your home bin.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see waste as a design problem, not only leftovers?

rubricLevels.secure: Uses expect … to or the passive.

objectives: Explain why recycling paper is important.
Describe the paper recycling process.
Explain how wood is recycled.
Use the present simple passive and so that.
content.pedagogy: The chapter describes processes, which makes it ideal for the present simple passive. A process flow chart (collect → press → transport → process) helps learners follow the steps.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Paper is pressed into blocks to make it easier to transport, not to make it dry.
Timber is wood that is ready to use.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: present simple passive (is collected, is pressed, is processed) · so that · which makes it + adjective
Notice (Activity 1): Paper waste is collected separately …
Build (Activities 2–3): order the process, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *is collect · *so that it not gets wet.
Use (Activity 4): describe a process.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens to the paper in our recycling box?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is recycling paper important?
Second reading: complete the flow chart.
Find what wood waste becomes.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Flow chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: describe a process; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why must paper stay dry?
Why is paper pressed into blocks?
Why is wood an important material?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Pressed into Blocks” and “Timber and Boards” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: raw materials, press, transport, process, cardboard, timber.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the flow chart with the first step written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the process for wood recycling in the passive.

formativeAssessment: Explains why recycling paper is important.
expectedResponses: Recycling paper saves a great amount of raw materials. Paper waste is collected separately so that it does not get wet. Then it is pressed into blocks and processed into new paper.
content.transferTask: Describe a recycling process at your school.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the passive for the process?

exitTicket: Write one step of paper recycling in the passive.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why recycling paper is important.

objectives: Explain why plastics cannot all be recycled in the same way.
Describe the changes in plastic production and waste.
Explain what happened to plastic waste.
Use rise from … to and the past simple passive.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is full of data. A bar chart (production vs waste, 2000 and 2019) and a pie chart (9 · 19 · 50 · 22) help learners read the numbers. The language of describing data is very useful at B1.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Plastic waste grew faster than plastic production.
Only 9 percent was recycled; the rest was burned, buried or left in nature.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: rise from … to … · an increase of … · past simple passive (was recycled, was burned)
Notice (Activity 1): It rose from 234 to 460 million tons …
Build (Activities 2–3): describe the data, then choose the forms.
Likely errors: *rose of 234 to 460 · *was burn.
Use (Activity 4): a data report.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Numbers: two hundred thirty-four; four hundred sixty million tons; ninety-seven percent.
Stress: pro-DUC-tion, IN-crease (noun), DUMPS.
beforeReading: Ask: “Where does plastic go at the end of its life?”
duringReading: First reading: Why can plastics not all be recycled in the same way?
Second reading: complete the bar chart and the pie chart.
Find where most plastic ended up.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Bar and pie charts; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a data report; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why can plastics not all be recycled in the same way?
Which grew faster: production or waste?
What happened to the plastic that escaped into nature?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Almost Doubled” and “Open Dumps” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: manufactured goods, global, production, double, landfill, dump, escape.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the charts with the labels written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short data report on plastic waste in 2019.

formativeAssessment: Explains why plastic is hard to recycle.
Uses rise from … to or the passive correctly.
expectedResponses: Between 2000 and 2019, plastic waste rose from 156 to 353 million tons. Only 9 percent was recycled, and half of it went into landfills.
content.transferTask: Write a data report about your school or town.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners read the numbers accurately?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “rose from … to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why plastic is hard to recycle.
Uses rise from … to or the passive.

objectives: Explain what glass is made from and how it is recycled.
Explain why glass is sorted by color.
Explain what composite packaging is.
Use made from, made by + -ing and for this reason.
content.pedagogy: The chapter compares a simple material (glass) with a complex one (composite packaging). A comparison chart (made from · how recycled · why special) helps learners see why composite packaging is harder to recycle.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Composite packaging has layers that must be separated; it is not simply paper.
Sorting by color keeps the quality of glass high.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be made from · be made by + -ing · for this reason · separate from
Notice (Activity 1): Glass is made mainly from … / Composite packaging is made by combining …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *made by combine · *separated of.
Use (Activity 4): how is it made?
beforeReading: Ask: “What is a juice carton made from?”
duringReading: First reading: How is glass recycled?
Second reading: complete the comparison chart.
Find why composite packaging creates a lot of waste.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Comparison chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: how is it made?; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is glass sorted by color?
How does glass recycling help the climate?
Why must composite waste be collected separately?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Sorted by Color” and “A Thin Layer” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: limestone, container, sort, carbon emissions, composite, combine, advanced.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that compares glass and composite packaging.

formativeAssessment: Uses made from or made by correctly.
expectedResponses: Glass is made mainly from sand, soda ash and limestone. It is sorted by color to keep its quality high. Composite packaging is made by combining paperboard, plastic and aluminum.
content.transferTask: Write about how a product is made and recycled.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain why composite packaging is harder to recycle?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “is made by …-ing”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses made from or made by.

objectives: Explain where metal comes from and how it is recycled.
Explain why recycling metal saves energy.
Explain what vegetable waste oil is and what it becomes.
Use must be + past participle and so that … can.
content.pedagogy: The chapter gives two processes with clear reasons. A reason chart (material → why collect separately → what it becomes) helps learners compare metal and oil.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Biodiesel is made from vegetable oil, not from fossil fuels.
“Much less energy” uses “less” because energy is uncountable.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: must be / can be + past participle · so that … can · much less … than
Notice (Activity 1): Metal waste must be collected separately so that it can be recovered.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *must collected · *fewer energy.
Use (Activity 4): kitchen rules.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: MIN-er-als, re-COV-ered, ex-pi-RA-tion, BI-o-die-sel, re-NEW-a-ble.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you do with used frying oil at home?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is metal recycled?
Second reading: complete the reason chart.
Find what waste oil becomes.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Reason chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: kitchen rules; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does recycling metal save energy?
What counts as vegetable waste oil?
Why is biodiesel called renewable?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Much Less Energy” and “Biodiesel” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: mineral, recover, mine, expiration date, pollute, renewable, biodiesel.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short leaflet about waste oil.

formativeAssessment: Uses must be or so that correctly.
expectedResponses: Metal waste must be collected separately so that it can be recovered. Recycling it needs much less energy than mining new metal. Waste oil can be turned into biodiesel.
content.transferTask: Write rules for waste in a school canteen.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners compare the two processes?

exitTicket: Write one rule with “must be + past participle”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses must be or so that.

objectives: Give examples of organic waste.
Explain where food is lost and where it is wasted.
Explain why each of us can make a difference.
Use surprisingly, in fact and as a result.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from general facts to a surprising personal one: most food waste happens at home. A food journey line (farm → shop → home) with the numbers helps learners see where food is lost and wasted.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Food is “lost” before it reaches the customer and “wasted” in homes, restaurants and shops.
61 percent is the share of food waste that happens in households.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: surprisingly · in fact · as a result · as well as · is lost / is wasted
Notice (Activity 1): Surprisingly, … In fact, …
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *In fact of · *Surprising, the answer …
Use (Activity 4): making a difference.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: or-GAN-ic, HAR-vest-ed, HOUSE-holds, sur-PRIS-ing-ly.
Numbers: thirteen point two percent; sixty-one percent.
beforeReading: Ask: “Where do you think most food waste happens?”
duringReading: First reading: What is organic waste?
Second reading: complete the food journey line.
Find where most food waste happens.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Food journey line; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: making a difference; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is the difference between lost and wasted food?
Why is the answer “our own homes” surprising?
How can each of us make a difference?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Scraps and Straw” and “Our Own Homes” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: play a role, scraps, straw, harvest, household, make a difference.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the food journey line with the places written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short news report about food waste.

formativeAssessment: Explains where food is lost and wasted.
expectedResponses: Organic waste includes fruit and vegetable scraps and straw. Surprisingly, most food waste happens at home. In fact, 61 percent of all food waste happens in households.
content.transferTask: Write about how your family can waste less food.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the numbers with their own homes?

exitTicket: Write one sentence that starts with “Surprisingly”.

objectives: Explain how electronic waste is recycled.
Explain how batteries work and why they need special bins.
Explain why recycling alone cannot solve the problem.
Use when, so that and instead of.
content.pedagogy: The chapter ends the first part of the book: it shows that even good recycling has limits. This prepares learners for the big idea of Zero Waste in Chapter 8. A “limits of recycling” box helps learners see the turn.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Toxic substances are removed before devices are taken apart.
Zero Waste does not stop recycling; it tries to stop waste before it is created.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: when (general situations) · so that · instead of + -ing · passive (are taken apart)
Notice (Activity 1): Instead of only managing waste, it tries to stop waste …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *instead of manage · *can leaks.
Use (Activity 4): the life of a phone.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: e-lec-TRON-ic, TOX-ic, SUB-stan-ces, LITH-i-um, CO-balt, NICK-el.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you do with an old phone?”
duringReading: First reading: How is electronic waste recycled?
Second reading: list the steps for batteries.
Find why recycling alone is not enough.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Battery steps; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: the life of a phone; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why must toxic substances be removed safely?
How do batteries work?
Why can recycling alone not solve the problem?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Toxic Substances” and “Lithium, Cobalt and Nickel” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: device, toxic, substance, take apart, rare, damaged, leak.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: When …, … / Instead of …-ing, …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that explains the turn from recycling to Zero Waste.

formativeAssessment: Explains how electronic waste is recycled.
Uses when, so that or instead of correctly.
expectedResponses: Electronic waste must be collected in separate bins so that its toxic substances can be removed safely. Recycling needs a lot of energy, so it cannot solve the problem alone. Instead of only managing waste, Zero Waste tries to stop it.
content.transferTask: Write about what should happen to an old phone.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the turn to Zero Waste?

rubricLevels.secure: Explains how electronic waste is recycled.
Uses when, so that or instead of.

objectives: Explain what Zero Waste really means.
Explain sustainability.
Explain why waste is a loss of resources.
Use might, is based on and which means.
content.pedagogy: The chapter corrects a common idea (“zero” = nothing) and introduces sustainability. A “myth / fact” chart helps learners compare the two ideas.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Zero Waste does not mean no trash at all.
Sustainability is about future generations as well as today.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: might (possibility) · be based on · which means + -ing · could …, and then we would …
Notice (Activity 1): … you might think they mean producing no trash at all.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *based in · *which means to meet.
Use (Activity 4): what Zero Waste means to me.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: sus-tain-a-BIL-i-ty, ap-PROACH, gen-er-A-tions, RE-sour-ces, re-SPON-si-bly.
beforeReading: Ask: “Does zero waste mean no waste at all?”
duringReading: First reading: What does Zero Waste really mean?
Second reading: complete the myth / fact chart.
Find why waste is a loss.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Myth / fact chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: what Zero Waste means to me; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is producing no trash at all impossible?
What is sustainability?
Why does the writer say we are throwing away valuable resources?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Sustainability” and “The Whole Life of a Product” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: effort, manage, sustainable, approach, resources, responsibly, eco-friendly.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the myth written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short definition of sustainability with an example.

formativeAssessment: Explains what Zero Waste really means.
Uses might or is based on correctly.
expectedResponses: You might think that zero waste means producing no trash at all, but that is impossible. The Zero Waste approach is based on sustainability, which means meeting our needs today without damaging resources for the future.
content.transferTask: Write about what Zero Waste means to you.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners correct the myth in their own words?

rubricLevels.secure: Uses might or is based on.

objectives: Explain the circular economy.
Explain why it is called “circular”.
Compare the circular and the linear economy.
Use instead and it is called … because.
content.pedagogy: The chapter defines the circular economy by comparison. Two diagrams (a line and a loop) on the board make the idea visual, and learners place each description on the right diagram.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The circular economy still allows economic growth, but it should not harm nature.
“Instead” comes after a negative idea.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: it is called … because · instead · is seen as · by + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): … do not move in a straight line … Instead, they move in a loop …
Build (Activities 2–3): sort the descriptions, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Instead of, they move … · *is called because of …
Use (Activity 4): a product in a loop.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the difference between a line and a loop?”
duringReading: First reading: What is a circular economy?
Second reading: draw the line and the loop.
Find the linear model.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Line and loop; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a product in a loop; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Zero Waste a bridge to a circular economy?
How does nature work?
What is the main goal?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “An Important Bridge” and “Take, Make, Waste” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: circular, bridge, aim, loop, growth, linear.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the two diagrams with the first steps written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that compares the two economies.

formativeAssessment: Uses instead or it is called … because correctly.
expectedResponses: A circular economy keeps products and materials in use for as long as possible. It is called “circular” because resources move in a loop. A linear economy follows a “take, make, waste” model.
content.transferTask: Write about one product in a linear and a circular economy.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners compare the two models clearly?

objectives: Explain the three principles.
Explain durable, repairable and upgradable products.
Explain the difference between recycling and upcycling.
Use should be + adjective / past participle and by + -ing.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is a list of principles with explanations. A three-box chart helps learners sort actions. Learners then design a better product, which links the principles with real life.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Recycling makes new materials; upcycling makes products of higher value.
Reduce comes first because it stops waste before it starts.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: should be + adjective · should be + past participle · by + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): Products should be designed to last a long time …
Build (Activities 2–3): sort the actions, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *should designed · *by use.
Use (Activity 4): design a better product.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do some things break so quickly?”
duringReading: First reading: What are the three principles?
Second reading: complete the three-box chart.
Find the difference between recycling and upcycling.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Three-box chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: design a better product; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Reduce the first principle?
What makes a product durable?
How does upcycling go one step further?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Durable Products” and “Higher Value” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: principle, design, durable, upgrade, upcycling, value.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the three headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short guide to the three principles.

formativeAssessment: Uses should be or by + -ing correctly.
expectedResponses: Reduce means stopping waste before it starts. Products should be durable and easy to repair. Upcycling turns waste into new products of higher value.
content.transferTask: Write about how a product should be designed.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate recycling and upcycling?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “should be designed”.

content.chapter: Chapter 11: Why Is the Circular Economy Important?
objectives: Explain the three benefits of the circular economy.
Explain how it supports sustainable growth.
Summarize the argument.
Use in short, as a result and comparative adverbs.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is a clear argument with three benefits and a summary. A benefit chart (benefit · how · result) helps learners see the structure and then write their own short argument.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The circular economy still supports growth; it is not against the economy.
“In short” summarizes; it does not add a new benefit.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in short · as a result · comparative adverbs (more efficiently) · not as many … as
Notice (Activity 1): In short, the circular economy is a promising new way …
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the words, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *more efficient (adverb needed) · *as many new resources than.
Use (Activity 4): benefits for our town.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why is the circular economy good for us?”
duringReading: First reading: What are the three benefits?
Second reading: complete the benefit chart.
Find the summary.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Benefit chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: benefits for our town; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does the circular economy reduce waste?
What does using resources efficiently mean?
Why will the circular economy become more important?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Better Use of Resources” and “New Jobs” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: benefit, efficiently, get rid of, cost, promising.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the three headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short argument with three benefits and a summary.

formativeAssessment: Uses in short or as a result correctly.
expectedResponses: The circular economy reduces waste and pollution, uses resources more efficiently and supports sustainable growth. In short, it is a promising new way of thinking about the economy.
content.transferTask: Write about the benefits of a repair café in your town.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the structure of the argument?

exitTicket: Write one sentence that starts with “In short”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses in short or as a result.

objectives: Explain how waste and the climate crisis are connected.
Explain what methane is and where it comes from.
Explain the injustice of climate change.
Use the present perfect and however.
content.pedagogy: The chapter links waste with climate in a chain (organic waste → landfill → methane → warming) and raises a question of justice. Learners give a reasoned opinion.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Methane comes from organic materials rotting in landfills.
Developing countries produce low emissions but suffer the most.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: present perfect (have more than doubled) · however / but · so
Notice (Activity 1): … emissions have more than doubled in the last 50 years.
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *have doubled 50 years ago · *However they suffer, but …
Use (Activity 4): is it fair?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: METH-ane, in-JUS-tice, de-VEL-op-ing, POL-lu-tants.
Numbers: fifteen to twenty percent.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens to food waste in a landfill?”
duringReading: First reading: How are waste and climate connected?
Second reading: complete the chain.
Find the injustice.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chain; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: is it fair?; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is methane?
How does Zero Waste stop harmful gases at the source?
Why is the situation unjust?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Methane” and “A Serious Injustice” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: crisis, greenhouse gas, rot, release, injustice, developing country, run out of, absorb.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain with the first step written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph about methane and black carbon.

formativeAssessment: Explains the link between waste and climate.
Uses the present perfect or however correctly.
expectedResponses: When organic materials rot in landfills, they release methane. Better waste management can cut emissions by 15 to 20 percent. However, developing countries often suffer the most from climate change.
content.transferTask: Write about the injustice of climate change.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners give a reasoned opinion?

exitTicket: Write one sentence that starts with “However”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the link between waste and climate.
Uses the present perfect or however.

objectives: Explain why we need to act before waste appears.
Explain how food waste can be reduced.
Explain why single-use packaging is not necessary.
Use can be replaced with and that is why.
content.pedagogy: The chapter turns from ideas to action. A “replace it” chart (single-use item → waste-free choice) helps learners plan practical changes.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Packaging-free shops help stop both packaging and food waste.
“Replace A with B”: A goes, B comes.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: can be replaced with · that is why · the passive (is never created)
Notice (Activity 1): … can all be replaced with waste-free choices.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *replaced by with · *That is because we need …
Use (Activity 4): a waste-free canteen.
beforeReading: Ask: “What single-use things did you use this week?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the best waste?
Second reading: complete the “replace it” chart.
Find where food waste can be reduced.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 “Replace it” chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a waste-free canteen; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is the best waste the waste that is never created?
Where can food waste be reduced?
Why is most single-use packaging not necessary?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Never Created” and “Waste-Free Choices” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: practical, single-use, replace, canteen, packaging-free.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the single-use items written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short leaflet with three practical ideas.

formativeAssessment: Uses can be replaced with correctly.
expectedResponses: The best waste is the waste that is never created. That is why we need to act before waste appears. Plastic water bottles can be replaced with waste-free choices.
content.transferTask: Write ideas for a waste-free school canteen.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners give practical, realistic ideas?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “can be replaced with”.

content.chapter: Chapter 14: Cities, Families and the Future
objectives: Explain what local governments can do.
Explain why teaching children and families is important.
Explain why Zero Waste is a journey.
Use where-clauses and no better time than now.

metadata.title: Zero Waste B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Our World Today
metadata.estimatedDuration: 14 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected informational texts about society, economy and the environment, and who can produce supported explanations and short arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through an informational text about waste and Zero Waste: kinds of waste and their recycling processes, the limits of recycling, sustainability, the circular economy, the three principles, waste and climate, and what people and cities can do, using the Language Focus attached to every chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 14 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a real object (a bottle, a carton, a battery) or a picture of a bin.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a number line, a process flow chart, data charts, a comparison chart, a myth / fact chart, a line and a loop, a benefit chart or a list of actions.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, a real object or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets, Key Terms and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the chapter sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: expect + object + to · present simple passive (is treated) · make up / end up
Ch2: present simple passive (is collected, is pressed, is processed) · so that · which makes it + adjective
Ch3: rise from … to … · an increase of … · past simple passive (was recycled, was burned)
Ch4: be made from · be made by + -ing · for this reason · separate from
Ch5: must be / can be + past participle · so that … can · much less … than
Ch6: surprisingly · in fact · as a result · as well as · is lost / is wasted
Ch7: when (general situations) · so that · instead of + -ing · passive (are taken apart)
Ch8: might (possibility) · be based on · which means + -ing · could …, and then we would …
Ch9: it is called … because · instead · is seen as · by + -ing
Ch10: should be + adjective · should be + past participle · by + -ing
Ch11: in short · as a result · comparative adverbs (more efficiently) · not as many … as
Ch12: present perfect (have more than doubled) · however / but · so
Ch13: can be replaced with · that is why · the passive (is never created)
Ch14: relative clauses with where · there is no better … than · not … but

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, facts, numbers and processes.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, processes, data, causes and results.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe processes, explain ideas and propose solutions.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D16 Responsibility — Caring for nature and future generations.
D5 Sensitivity — Noticing what nature needs.
D20 Helpfulness — Sharing and helping others.
languageFocus: Every one of the 14 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, real objects, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside numbers or opinions.
Talk about food waste and money with care; some families may have little food at home.
Do not let learners touch real batteries or broken electronics in class; use pictures or closed, clean objects.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Zero Waste connects with questions every community faces today: how to use less, how to share and repair, and how to protect nature together.

themes.title: Need and greed:
themes.description: Gandhi said the world has enough for everyone’s need, but not for everyone’s greed (Chapter 14). Discuss what this means in your culture.

themes.title: Sharing:
themes.description: Tool libraries let people borrow tools instead of buying them (Chapter 14). Discuss how neighbors share things in your community.

themes.title: Fairness:
themes.description: Developing countries often suffer the most from climate change (Chapter 12). Discuss how countries can help each other.

themes.title: Future generations:
themes.description: Sustainability protects the resources that future generations will need (Chapter 8). Discuss what we owe to people in the future.

miniProject.title: Zero Waste: A Town Plan
miniProject.desc: In groups, each member becomes an expert on one part of the book: materials, ideas, benefits or action. Teach your part, then write a town plan with four actions.

reflectivePrompt.title: My Zero Waste Journey

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D16 Responsibility

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can read straightforward factual texts on subjects related to his/her field and interest with a satisfactory level of comprehension.
practice: Chapter 3 (Plastic): Read and describe the data.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write straightforward connected texts on a range of familiar subjects within his field of interest, by linking a series of shorter discrete elements into a linear sequence.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

metadata.title: Zero Waste B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the text about Zero Waste alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 14 chapters of Zero Waste.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Describe how different kinds of waste are recycled.
Explain Zero Waste, sustainability and the circular economy with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 14.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One idea about waste that changed the way I think:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 14 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows responsibility, sensitivity, helpfulness and justice. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Responsibility: Responsibility: Sustainability means meeting our needs today without damaging the resources that future generations will need (Chapter 8).
Sensitivity: Sensitivity: Waste batteries must be collected in special bins because their dangerous chemicals can leak into the soil and water (Chapter 7).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Tool libraries let people borrow tools instead of buying them (Chapter 14).
Justice: Justice: Many developing countries produce very low emissions, but they often suffer the most from climate change (Chapter 12).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 14, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Key Facts
Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Key Terms
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in five sentences what Zero Waste means and why it matters, in your home language or in English.
